content.body: Ever wondered how old phone keypads work for texting? Each number corresponds to multiple letters. Today we'll solve a classic problem: generating all possible letter combinations from a phone number. You'll learn to use backtracking with a lookup structure to build combinations efficiently.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply backtracking to generate all possible combinations
• Implement a digit-to-letters mapping using an object
• Explain how the recursion builds combinations step by step
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple example. For the digit '2' on a phone keypad, which letters does it represent?
content.title: Try it
Try two digits
content.prompt: What are all possible two-letter combinations for digits '23'?
content.successMessage: Great! You found all 9 combinations by pairing each letter of '2' with each letter of '3'.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: What about digits '234'? How many three-letter combinations total?
content.successMessage: Exactly! 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 combinations. You systematically combined letters from each digit.

content.body: What you just did was explore all possibilities manually. For each digit, you tried every corresponding letter and combined them. This is the essence of generating combinations.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the input has 7 digits (like '2345678'), manually writing all combinations becomes impossible—there could be thousands! We need a systematic method that a computer can execute efficiently. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: We need to remember what letters each digit maps to, then build combinations step by step. Think of it like a notebook where we write down the mapping (digit → letters) and use it to construct combinations without re-scanning. We'll store the mapping as keys (digits) and values (letter strings).
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll use backtracking with a lookup object. For each digit, get its letters from the mapping, add each letter to the current combination, then move to the next digit recursively.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
For '23': Start with empty combination ''.
Digit '2' → letters 'abc'. Try 'a', move to next digit.
Digit '3' → letters 'def'. Try 'd' → combination 'ad', save it. Backtrack, try 'e' → 'ae', etc.
After exploring all letters of '3', backtrack to '2', try 'b', repeat.

content.body:
1. Create a mapping object: digit → corresponding letters
2. Define a recursive function that takes current combination and next digit index
3. Base case: if we've processed all digits, save the combination
4. For current digit, get its letters from mapping
5. For each letter, append to combination, recurse with next index, then backtrack
6. Start recursion with empty combination and index 0
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the digit-letter mapping
steps.instruction: Define an object that maps each digit (2-9) to its corresponding letters as a string. This is our lookup structure.
steps.expectedOutcome: An object with keys '2' through '9' and corresponding letter strings.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've created the lookup structure we'll use throughout.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure to include all digits 2-9 with their correct letters.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need an object where each digit key maps to its letters.

steps.title: Initialize result array and check edge case
steps.instruction: Create an empty array to store all combinations. If the input is empty, return an empty array immediately.
steps.hint: Check if digits.length === 0 and return [] if true.
steps.expectedOutcome: An empty array for results and early return for empty input.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the result container and handled the edge case.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Don't forget to return the empty array for empty input.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: create a results array and check if digits is empty.

steps.title: Define the recursive backtracking function
steps.instruction: Create a helper function named backtrack that takes two parameters: current combination string and current index in digits.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function definition for backtrack with two parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! The backtrack function is the core of our solution.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure it takes both combination and index parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again: define a function named backtrack with two parameters.

steps.title: Add base case to backtrack
steps.instruction: Inside backtrack, check if we've processed all digits. If index equals digits.length, push the current combination to result and return.
steps.expectedOutcome: Base case that saves complete combinations and returns.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! This stops recursion when we have a full combination.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Check if index equals digits.length and save the combination.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: when we've processed all digits, save the combination.

steps.title: Process current digit and recurse
steps.instruction: Get the letters for the current digit using our map. Loop through each letter, append it to combination, recurse with index+1, then backtrack by removing the letter.
steps.hint: const letters = map[digits[index]]; for (let letter of letters) { backtrack(combination + letter, index + 1); }
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that gets letters for current digit and recurses for each letter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! This explores all possible letter choices for each digit.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Remember to get letters from map using digits[index].
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: get letters for current digit, loop through them, and recurse.

steps.title: Start recursion and return result
steps.instruction: Call backtrack with empty string and index 0, then return the result array.
steps.expectedOutcome: Initial call to backtrack and return of final result.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've completed the solution. The recursion will generate all combinations.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost done. Don't forget to call backtrack and return the result.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: start the recursion with empty string and index 0, then return result.

content.body: Great work! You've implemented the Letter Combinations of a Phone Number solution using backtracking with a lookup object. Remember: the mapping object lets us quickly access letters for each digit without re-scanning, and backtracking systematically builds all combinations. This pattern of 'remembering mappings' and 'exploring all possibilities' appears in many algorithm problems.
